 In The Court Of Sh. Ashu Garg,

sentences.text:
1. The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954
(Pfa Act), alleging that the accused has violated the provisions of the Pfa Act and Rules.

The
acc
used Dhani Ram is stated to be the vendor-cum-proprietor of M/s. Bikaner Sweets, from where the food article, that is, 'Laddoo' was lifted for sampling.

2. As per the complaint, on 18.10.2006, the food officials consisting of Food Inspector (FI) V.P.S.
Chaudhary and Field Assistant (FA) Balwant Sah under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. K.K. Sharma reached along with their staff at the premises of M/s. Bikaner Sweets at WZ-101, Chand Nagar, Tilak Nagar, New Delhi-110018, where the accused Dhani Ram was found conducting the business of various food articles including laddoo, which were lying in an open tray meant for sale for human consumption.
The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of 'Laddoo' from the said vendor, to which he agreed.
The sample was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules.

Each sample was separately packed,
fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the notice as per Form-VI, panchnama, etc.
The price of sample was paid to the vendor.
Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.
Vide report dated 08.11.2006, the PA found the sample to be adulterated because total dye content of synthetic colour was exceeding the prescribed maximum limit of 100 ppm.
Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by FI.
After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.

The complaint was then filed in the court on 09.05.2007 alleging In Re vs Sh. Dhani Ram on 5 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150631976/
1 violation of section 2(ia)(a)(j) and (m) of PFA Act read with Rules 28, 29 and 30 of PFA Rules , as punishable section 7/16(1A) of PFA Act.
3.

sentences.text: As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused was summoned vide order dated 09.05.2007.

The accused appeared but never opted to file any application under section 13(2) of PFA Act thereby exercising his right to get the second counterpart of the sample to be analysed from Central Food Laboratory (CFL).
4.
Based on the PA report, pre-charge evidence was recorded wherein the complainant examined PW-1 FI V. P. S. Chaudhary.

On the basis of his testimony, charge was framed against the accused on 20.05.2011 for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1A) PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ia)(j) and (m) of PFA Act, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.

Thereafter, the witness already examined in pre-charge stage was recalled for further cross-examination in post-charge stage and additionally, PW-2 FA Balwant Sah and PW-3 Sh. K. K.
Sharma (SDM/LHA) were examined in post-charge stage.
5. PW-1, PW-2 and PW-3 were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings.

All these witnesses deposed about the steps undertaken by them for lifting the sample and also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex. PW-1/A, notice in Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B,
Panchnama Ex. PW-1/C, PA receipt Ex. PW-1/D and LHA receipt Ex. PW-1/E. PA report Ex.
PW-1/F was received which opined the sample to be adulterated.
Based on the report, investigation was carried out by PW-1 who wrote letter Ex. PW-1/G to the vendor but no reply was received.
He also wrote letter Ex. PW-1/H to the STO ward no. 57 to ascertain the constitution of the business concern and it was replied that no such firm was registered.

After completion of investigation,
consent Ex. PW-1/I was obtained from the then Director, PFA and thereafter, complaint Ex. PW-1/J was filed in the court.
Intimation letter Ex. PW-1/K along with copy of PA report were sent to the accused through post.
These witnesses were duly cross-examined by the defence wherein they denied that the accused had nothing to do with the business concern or that he has been falsely implicated.
6. Statement of the accused under section 313 Cr.PC was recorded on 31.07.2014 wherein he denied the allegations.
He stated that he had no relation with the business concern M/s. Bikaner Sweets and also that no intimation letter was received by him.
He stated that the said shop was being run at that time by one Sh. Ravinder from whom sample was lifted a few days prior to the incident.
Then on the day of incident, PFA staff was again presnet there and were threatening the said Ravinder when the accused intervened which infuriated the team.
This led to false implication of the accused despite the fact that he had no relation with the shop in question.
He sought to lead evidence in defence.
7. The accused examined one Sh. Naresh Baghel as DW-1.
However, his cross-examination was deferred but he was never brought to witness box thereafter.
As such, his statement remained incomplete and no part of such statement can be read in evidence.

In Re vs Sh. Dhani Ram on 5 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150631976/
2
8. Accused also examined one Sh. Attar Singh as DW-2.

He deposed that the property no. WZ-101,
Chand Nagar (shop in question) belonged to one Mam Chand (since expired) and the shop was being run on rent by one Ravinder who has since closed the shop and his whereabouts were not known.
He claimed that accused never had any relation with Bikaner Sweet shop, though his house was opposite that shop.

9. In these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the prosecution has been able to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt against the accused as he has not been able to rebut the findings of the PA report and has also failed to establish his defence.
10. On the other hand, Ld. Legal Aid Counsel has submitted that there are various missing links in the testimony of witnesses.
Ld. Counsel has strongly contended that there is no evidence to connect the accused to the shop in question.
He submits that the present is a case of false implication by the PFA officials.
11. I have heard the arguments as advanced by both the sides and have carefully perused the material available on record.
12. The charge framed against the accused is for violation of section 2(ia)(j) and (m) of the PFA Act read with Rules 28, 29, and 30 of PFA Rules.
Section 2(ia)(j) specifically deals with colouring matter which is present other than prescribed or is present beyond the prescribed limits of variability.

Section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act deals with situation where the quality or purity of an article falls below the prescribed standard or its constituents are present in quantities not within the prescribed limits of variability.
Under Rule 28, list of permitted synthetic food colours is provided which can be used in prescribed limits.
Rule 29 provides list of food articles in which such colours are permitted to be used.
Rule 30 provides the maximum limit up to which such colours can be used in the prescribed food articles.
In the case at hand, it is submitted that the food colour used in laddoos was upto 141.68 ppm, which was beyond the permissible limit of 100 ppm.
13. However, the defence of the accused is not with respect to the existence of such adulteration.

The only ground urged by the Ld. Defence Counsel is that there is nothing on record to connect the accused Dhani Ram to the business concern M/s. Bikaner Sweets from where the food article in question was lifted for sampling.

14. In this regard, the prosecution case is based on the evidence of three witnesses PW-1, PW-2 and PW-3 who identified the accused to be the one who was found present at the premises of M/s.
Bikaner Sweets at WZ-101, Chand Nagar, Tilak Nagar, New Delhi where he was conducting the business of various food articles.
15. It is to be noted that the prosecution case is based only on the testimony of the officials of the PFA department.
There is no person other than the team members who have testified against the accused.

Though all the three witnesses stated in a stereotype manner that they had requested some passers-by, consumers and neighbouring shopkeepers to join as witnesses but none had agreed, yet such a version is not free from doubt.

The court is well aware that these witnesses cannot be termed In Re vs Sh. Dhani Ram on 5 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150631976/
3 as interested witnesses or their testimony unreliable merely because they happen to be PFA officials.

However, it is equally true that when such case is based only on the evidence of such witnesses,
despite the presence of independent public witnesses, the court is required to remain extra cautious while appreciating their testimony.

No doubt such officials are competent witnesses but to rely only on their testimony in the absence of any corroboration from an independent public witness, their testimony has to remain unblemished and credible enough so as to convict a person for a criminal offence.
16. In the present case, serious infirmities / missing links are there in the prosecution case which would compel the court not to rely only on the testimony of the three witnesses blindly.

Apparently,
it does not appeal to senses that every public person including passers-by or customers or even the neighbouring shopkeepers would simply refuse to join the sample proceedings when directed by the food officials.
The identity of such witnesses were never recorded nor any notice was given to them in writing nor any action was taken against them for such refusal.
It is not that no such person was available.
Rather it is submitted that no such person agreed to join as witness despite attempt.

The court can understand the reluctance of public persons in joining such legal proceedings and in swuch case, the court would have ordinarily believed the testimony of PFA officials as well, but because of the reasons to be discussed below, the court is not inclined to do so in the present case.

17. It is important to note that except the oral testimony of the three witness, that the accused was found present at the spot and conducting the business at the shop in question, there is no substantive and unimpeachable evidence on the basis of which the court may conclude that the accused had anything to do with the business concern M/s. Bikaner Sweets.
18. Apparently, the accused was a resident of the same locality where the shop in question was situated.
His residential address and address of the shop in question, coupled with the testimony of DW-2 would make it clear that the accused was a resident of same locality.
Therefore, his presence at the shop in question cannot be absolutely disbelieved otherwise and it cannot be made a reason to doubt the purpose of his presence.
In such a case, mere presence of the accused in the said area, or even at the shop in question, would not be incriminating enough per se.
But other than this, there is no evidence otherwise to show the involvement of the accused.
The accused had been maintaining from the very beginning that he had nothing to do with the said business concern.
Such a stand was taken during the cross-examination of the PWs, in the statement of the accused and also in defence evidence.
With such a consistent stand of the accused, the evidence of the PFA officials has to be viewed with minute circumspection.
19. Visibly, there is no documentary evidence on the basis of which the court may establish the link between the accused and the business concern M/s. Bikaner Sweets.
Admittedly, no document prepared at the spot bears the signatures of the accused.
The vendor's receipt, notice in Form VI and panchnama prepared at the spot do not bear the signatures of the accused.
In this regard, it is the stand of the PWs that the accused had refused to sigh those documents.

Well,
if the accused had refused to sign those documents at the spot, it was the bounden and onerous duty on the part of the FI to collect all the relevant material, from the spot at the time of lifting the sample In Re vs Sh. Dhani Ram on 5 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150631976/
4 or even subsequently during the investigation, to establish the link of the accused with the business concern in question.
It was his duty to establish if the accused was the owner of the business concern or proprietor thereof or manager or an employee or a servant working at the said premises.
20. However, the is constrained to note that no such material was collected by the FI to establish the role of the accused viz-a-viz the shop in question.

No attempt was made by the FI to determine as to who was the landlord / owner of the premises in question, whether the shop running at the premises was a proprietorship concern or a partnership firm or a company and who was/were its proprietor,
partners or directors.
It is not known who all were working there and on what basis it has been claimed that the accused was found conducting the business there.

No statement of any owner /
proprietor / partner was recorded.
No statement of any worker / employee / helper who might be working at the shop has been recorded to show the job profile of accused.
It is not known as to in what capacity the accused was found working there, whether as owner or servant.

No bill book,
account books, ledgers, letter head, phone bills, electricity bill, postal record, payment receipts,
delivery challans or any other similar documents were lifted from the spot which might go to establish that the accused had anything to do with the shop in question.

Even if the accused had refused to sign the documents prepared by the FI, FI ought to have seized the relevant documents / books to establish the capacity in which the accused was found present at the spot.
Mere presence of the accused at the spot is not sufficient to established a case and it cannot be said that he was conducting the business or was responsible to ensure compliance of PFA rules.
21. Not only this, there is a serious missing link even at the stage of investigation.
According to PW-1, a letter Ex. PW-1/G was written to the vendor / accused.
A perusal of this letter would show that the same was sent only at the first address 'M/s. Bikaner Sweets, WZ-101, Chand Nagar, Tilak Nagar, New Delhi - 18'.

There is no reason why this letter was not sent by the FI to the residential address of the accused 'WZ-142, Chand Nagar, Tilak Nagar, New Delhi - 18'.
22.
It is to be noted that the FI was well aware of the residential address of the accused.
The panchnama Ex. PW-1/C which was prepared at the spot by the FI himself duly mentioned the correct residential address of the accused, that is, WZ-142, Chand Nagar, Tilak Nagar, New Delhi - 18.
The consent order Ex. PW-1/I also mentions both the addresses of the accused.
The complaint also mentions both these addresses.

When the FI was aware of the address of the accused, it is not explained as to why the letter was not sent to the accused at this address so as to ensure its delivery and to enable the accused to respond.

Apparently, when the accused had no concern with the said business concern, he would not have received the said letter Ex. PW-1/G sent at the address of the shop and therefore, he was not having any opportunity to reply to it.

In such a position, failure of the FI to send the letter at the admittedly correct address of the accused, would create further doubt in the case, particularly when the accused has been able to raise serious concern with respect to his association with the business concern M/s. Bikaner Sweets.
23. Not only this, the FI while deposing as PW-1 claimed that he had sent letter Ex. PW-1/H to the Sales Tax Office Ward No. 57 and as per reply, no such firm was found registered with Sales Tax.
Such a testimony is absolutely false and the inference sought be drawn through it is damaging.

The In Re vs Sh. Dhani Ram on 5 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150631976/
5 said letter Ex. PW-1/H had been written by the FI to the STO Ward No. 57 to seek information regarding constitution of M/s. Bikaner Sweets at WZ-101, Chand Nagar, Tilak Nagar, New Delhi - 18.
It was specifically questioned if the establishment was registered in that ward and if so, the name of the proprietor / partners with their particulars.
Reply to this letter was given by the STO at its bottom with the endorsement "This dealer not working in Ward 57".
24. Thus, this is not a case where the STO replied that the firm was not registered with Sales Tax department.
Rather it shows the conduct of the FI who sent the letter to STO of a different ward than the one where the shop in question fell.
The only reply given by the STO is, that the dealer in question was not in their ward and thus, the STO was not having the details of its proprietor/partners.
There is nothing to show that this business concern was not registered with the Sales Tax, as deposed by the FI.
The FI acted in a rather strange manner, which puts a question mark over the fairness in investigation.

When it was replied that the shop did not fall in Ward No.
57, it was obvious that no information would be available with the STO Ward No. 57 and it was then the duty of the FI to ascertain the correct ward number in which the business concern fell and then to ascertain its details afresh.
But strangely, the FI chose not to conduct any investigation further and without any basis, he claims to have assumed the accused to be the proprietor of the shop.

The FI had sought information from the different ward in which the business concern actually fell,
deliberately or negligently.
No explanation has been given by the FI as to what steps he took after receipt of such a reply from the STO and on what basis he claimed the accused to be a proprietor of the said shop.

If the FI had ascertained the correct ward number and the concerned STO had given some reply, the court would have been able to ascertain if the accused was the proprietor of the shop and if not, who was the proprietor.
But the conduct of the FI has left a serious missing link and rather created a dent in the prosecution case.

25. In view of the above mentioned inherent defect and infirmities, it is safe to conclude that the material on record is not sufficient to connect the accused to the business concern M/s. Bikaner Sweets so as to hold him responsible for any food article lifted from that shop.

This is more so in view of the evidence of DW-2 who withstood the test of cross- examination and stated that the accused had nothing to do with the said shop, that the accused used to sell fruits and vegetables on a cart near the said shop that belonged to one Choudhary Mam Chand who had since expired, that the said shop was being run on rent by one Ravinder and that the said shop has since been closed.
26. The prosecution case has serious infirmities and the conduct of the FI is not up to the mark.

It is the cardinal principle of criminal law that it is the duty of the prosecution to establish its case beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt and to prove the facts by bringing positive and credible evidence.
This burden has to be discharged by the prosecution itself and never shifts upon the accused.

27. When doubt has been created as aforesaid, the court need not go into other facts to ascertain if the sample proceedings were correct, if the PA report was correct, or if adulteration in the food article has been proved.
The evidence on record is not sufficient to conclude that the accused is connected to any such shop or offence.

In Re vs Sh. Dhani Ram on 5 September, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150631976/
6 28.
Having said so, the accused is given the benefit of doubt and is acquitted of the charges.

However, his bail bonds shall remain in force for the next six months in terms of section 437-A.
CrPC.
29.
File be consigned to record room.

Announced in the open court this 5rd day of September 2016 ASHU GARG ACMM-II (New Delhi),
